text: The address and spenders queries are the only ones that are not strictly bounded to a small size by consensus. However the spenders query is only pulling conflicts (double spends), so it's effectively limited by fee rate. The address query however can get very large results. The largest address on the chain is `1HckjUpRGcrrRAtFaaCAUaGjsPx9oYmLaZ`, which returns `5,179,483 outputs`. This is a `178MB` result in raw form. On a warm node this takes `7 secs` to generate, which includes enumeration via the address table multimap, and lookup of each tx's hash and the output offset, to generate the output point, and the full buffering of the result. On a cold node it takes `2.7 min` (mostly SSD read). There's no caching involved in the warm server, so with the chain memory resident, the warm time is close to the initial time.

elements.text:
Cancellability is now implemented in the address queries of the explore endpoint. I've got a little more organizing to do (push a couple calls into the database), but I consider this endpoint complete (for http, not yet https or ws/wss).

Without cancellation, a query initiated by a client (e.g. browser) would keep running until complete, even after the connection was closed, either by the caller disconnecting, a channel timeout, or a node stop. This is always the case, but with all queries in the few ms range it wasn't an issue. But the address queries are essentially unbounded, and can take minutes for the largest addresses. So now these queries are executed off of the channel strand, and are passed a reference to
which is updated in the strand:
So now these query terminations are immediate for anything that cases a channel stop.

I noticed that queries are not stopped/suspended/delayed when a snapshot is underway. At first I thought it was an issue, but then remembered that snapshots don't block read access to the store... so these just run concurrently with no problems.

Chrome remains unable to present the json (aw snap). Chrome renders the base16 text format in `3.6 mins`, which is funny since we produce it (end-to-end, warm server) in < `20 secs`. elements.text: Sorting the result set is important in that it ensures the same result is provided by the query from any server (caching and fingerprinting affected). Also it's not just sorting but deduplication, which is important given the distinct possibility of duplicate txs.

elements.text: I just implemented vectorization over the most costly part of the address queries. This requires the extra cost of collecting the output links into a vector first, so it's less efficient for small queries, but it cuts the large query times in half. Considering that the link collection is sequential, as is the sort/de-dup/serialization, that's a pretty large reduction in the query cost. 5.2 million now in 15 seconds. With modern cores that will be under 10 seconds easy - for the largest query possible.

In the past hour I added this config setting:
```[database]
turbo = true```
Parsed it in node config (defaulted false), passed it to database, exposed to queries, it via store, conditioned the address queries on it.
...
And added this query string option:
```?turbo[=true]```
Parsed it in node's explore query string, added it as an optional argument to the explore interface address methods (defaulted false), added it to each of the address interface handlers, passed it to the parallel invokers, and into the queries.
...
So the node can be configured to enable turbo, and if enabled a caller can request it via the query string in the expectation that the result set is large. Small queries will be faster without it, but probably not noticeably so.
...
An thus the `turbo` button was reborn!

elements.text: The caller disconnect scenario was not handled, but the process close scenario was. This is because on a process close the socket is terminated by the stop handler, which is ultimately invoked by the

event handler. But the caller disconnect is a per-channel signal that comes from the socket, and is only picked up by an async read handler being invoked. But while we are handling a call, there is no read handler pending. We resubscribe to the channel upon call completion. So even though the work is off strand, there was nothing to capture the close until the call completed. I resolved this by creating an

method on the socket, which will pick up termination. The challenge was cleanly registering and deregistering this before and after the potentially long-running calls. That's all done and working now.

text: The caller disconnect scenario was not handled, but the process close scenario was. But the caller disconnect is a per-channel signal that comes from the socket, and is only picked up by an async read handler being invoked. But while we are handling a call, there is no read handler pending. We resubscribe to the channel upon call completion. So even though the work is off strand, there was nothing to capture the close until the call completed. I resolved this by creating an `async_wait` method on the socket, which will pick up termination. The challenge was cleanly registering and deregistering this before and after the potentially long-running calls. That's all done and working now.

Note that we are the only node that was tested over an Internet connection.

According to his tracking, we download about 2.5% more than others. This is the result of aggressively dropping peers with blocks partially transmitted. Otherwise we don't perform any redundant downloading of blocks.

Also I was able to verify that despite the 32GB RAM, the maps were thrashing due to low CPU (12 slow threads). We'll need to do some more testing to find out where the CPU limit should be set for a 32GB machine.
